title: Newborns needing additional care
blurb: Keep mothers and babies together through transitional care, recognise early-onset neonatal infection with NICE NG195, manage low blood glucose and feeding problems, and escalate with NEWTT2.
question: Baby Tomi was born at 39 weeks after membranes had been ruptured for 30 hours. At 3 hours old he is grunting with a respiratory rate of 70 and is reluctant to feed. What should the midwife do?

teach.h: Additional care, without separation where possible
teach.body: Formally (BAPM 2017): neonatal transitional care (NTC) is care additional to normal infant care, provided in a postnatal clinical environment by the mother or another resident carer, supported by trained healthcare professionals. In plain English: many babies who need a little extra help (antibiotics, tube feeds, phototherapy, glucose checks) can stay with their mother instead of going to the neonatal unit. BAPM calls keeping mothers and babies together 'the cornerstone of newborn care'.

head: Type
Risk factor

Invasive GBS in a previous baby, or maternal GBS colonisation, bacteriuria or infection this pregnancy
Rupture of membranes over 18 h before a preterm birth, or over 24 h before a term birth
Suspected or confirmed maternal sepsis, or chorioamnionitis

children.label: Investigate and start antibiotics

children.label: Clinical judgement
children.sub: If monitoring: at least 12 h with a newborn early warning system

teach.caption: First line: benzylpenicillin with gentamicin (1.20.1). Stop at 36 hours if the blood culture is negative, initial suspicion was not strong, the baby is well and CRP is reassuring (1.21.3).

teach.h: NEWTT2 total score and response (BAPM, Nov 2023)

teach.body: Babies at risk (for example maternal diabetes, preterm, growth restricted, maternal beta-blockers) feed early and at least 3-hourly, with a first glucose before the second feed (2-4 hours). BAPM: treat a value under 1.0 mmol/L at any time, a single value under 2.5 with abnormal signs, or more than two values under 2.0 in a baby without signs; 40% glucose gel 200 mg/kg for 1.0 to 1.9. Babies with or at risk of infection can usually keep breastfeeding; support expressing if they cannot feed (NG195 1.1.5).

teach.h: Scenario: baby Tomi at 3 hours old
items: Risk factor: membranes ruptured over 24 hours before a term birth. Indicators: grunting, fast breathing, poor feeding.
That is 2 or more non-red-flag factors, so NG195 says investigate and start antibiotics without waiting for results.
The midwife calculates a NEWTT2 score, calls for urgent neonatal review and documents her observations.
Tomi is examined; cultures are taken and benzylpenicillin with gentamicin is given within 1 hour of the decision.
He is stable, so he has IV antibiotics in transitional care, staying with his mother, who is supported to breastfeed.

teach.text: Don't separate mother and baby by reflex. A clinically stable baby on IV antibiotics, tube feeds or phototherapy can often be cared for in transitional care with the mother as primary carer. And don't wait for blood culture results before starting antibiotics when NG195 criteria are met.

items: Transitional care: extra care with the mother resident, e.g. 34+0-35+6 weeks, 1600-2000 g, stable on IV antibiotics or tube feeds.
NG195 red flags: apnoea, seizures, CPR, ventilation, shock, or infection in a co-twin.
Any red flag or 2+ other factors: antibiotics within 1 hour, benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin.
One factor: clinical judgement; monitor at least 12 h with a newborn early warning system if needed.
Hypoglycaemia: first check before the second feed; treat under 1.0, under 2.5 with signs, or more than two under 2.0.

summary: You can now decide when a baby can stay with their mother in transitional care, recognise risk factors and clinical indicators of early-onset infection, and apply the NG195 antibiotic framework. You can also respond to NEWTT2 scores and manage low blood glucose and feeding difficulties.

A.q: Which of these is a 'red flag' clinical indicator of early-onset neonatal infection in NICE NG195?
A.why: NG195 box 2: red flag clinical indicators are apnoea, seizures, need for CPR, need for mechanical ventilation and signs of shock.

whyNot.0: Jaundice within 24 hours is a non-red-flag indicator; at 30 hours it is not on the list.
whyNot.1: The temperature indicator is under 36°C or over 38°C; 37.6°C is neither, so it is not an indicator.
whyNot.2: Feeding difficulty is an 'other' (non-red-flag) clinical indicator.

A.q: A baby has two non-red-flag risk factors for early-onset infection. What does NICE NG195 recommend?
A.why: NG195 1.10.3: with any red flag, or 2 or more non-red-flag risk factors or indicators, investigate and start antibiotics without waiting for test results.

whyNot.0: Observation with clinical judgement is for a single factor without red flags.
whyNot.1: Routine care is for babies with no risk factors or indicators.
whyNot.3: NICE says do not wait for test results before starting antibiotics.

A.q: Which first-line antibiotic regimen does NG195 recommend for suspected early-onset neonatal infection?
A.why: NG195 1.20.1: benzylpenicillin with gentamicin is first line for suspected early-onset infection.

whyNot.1: Co-amoxiclav is not the NG195 first-line choice.
whyNot.2: Erythromycin is used for P-PROM in the mother, not neonatal treatment.
whyNot.3: This is not the NG195 first-line regimen for early-onset infection.

B.q: A clinically stable baby born at 35+2 weeks weighing 2,250 g needs IV antibiotics for maternal risk factors. Where is the most appropriate place of care?
B.why: BAPM NTC criteria include babies 34+0 to 35+6 weeks and stable babies with risk factors needing IV antibiotics, cared for with their resident mother.

whyNot.0: A stable late preterm baby does not need intensive care.
whyNot.1: Separating mother and baby is avoidable when transitional care can meet the baby's needs.
whyNot.2: A paediatric ward would separate mother and baby; BAPM places this care in a postnatal setting with the mother resident.

B.q: A baby's NEWTT2 total score is 4. What response does the BAPM framework require?
B.why: NEWTT2 (Nov 2023): a score of 4-5 requires review within 15 minutes.

whyNot.0: Repeating observations within 1 hour is the response to a score of 1.
whyNot.1: Tier 1 review within 1 hour is for a score of 2-3.
whyNot.3: A score of 4 needs urgent review, not routine observations.

B.q: A baby of a mother with diabetes has a pre-feed blood glucose of 1.6 mmol/L at 3 hours. He is feeding and has no abnormal signs. What is the most appropriate first treatment?
options: Admit to NICU for IV fluids
B.why: BAPM: for a glucose of 1.0 to 1.9 mmol/L in a baby without abnormal signs, give 40% glucose gel 200 mg/kg alongside a feed, then recheck.

whyNot.1: Immediate IV glucose is not the first step for a well, feeding baby at 1.6; gel and feeding support come first.
whyNot.2: Any treatment for low glucose must be followed by a recheck.
whyNot.3: A well baby with 1.6 mmol/L can usually stay with his mother on gel and feeding support.

C.q: Baby Ella was born at 38 weeks; her mother had GBS bacteriuria this pregnancy. Ella is well, feeding and has normal observations. What does NG195 advise?
C.why: One non-red-flag risk factor without clinical indicators: use clinical judgement on whether to withhold antibiotics and whether to monitor; if monitoring, continue for at least 12 hours with a newborn early warning system (NG195 1.10.3).

whyNot.0: Immediate antibiotics are for a red flag or 2 or more factors.
whyNot.2: A risk factor is present, so clinical judgement and possible monitoring are needed, not routine care.
whyNot.3: A well baby with one risk factor does not need neonatal unit admission.

C.q: A baby on IV antibiotics for suspected infection is well at 36 hours, with negative blood cultures and a reassuring CRP. What does NG195 suggest?
options: Switch to oral antibiotics for 5 days
C.why: NG195 1.21.3: stop antibiotics at 36 hours if the blood culture is negative, the initial suspicion of infection was not strong, the baby is well with no clinical indicators, and CRP levels and trends are reassuring.

whyNot.0: A 7-day course is for a positive blood culture, or a negative one when sepsis was strongly suspected (1.21.1); this baby is well with reassuring results.
whyNot.1: Switching to oral antibiotics is not indicated when infection has not been confirmed.
whyNot.2: NICE sets 36 hours as the point to stop when the criteria are met, not 72 hours.

C.q: Baby Kai, in transitional care for IV antibiotics, is too sleepy to breastfeed well. His mother is upset she will have to stop breastfeeding. What is the best response?
options: Move him to the NNU for tube feeds
Advise waiting until he is discharged
C.why: NG195 1.1.5: reassure parents that babies with or at risk of infection can usually continue to breastfeed; if a baby is temporarily unable to breastfeed, support expressing breast milk.

whyNot.0: Antibiotics are not a reason to stop breastfeeding.
whyNot.2: Tube feeds of expressed milk can be given in transitional care; NNU transfer would separate them unnecessarily.
whyNot.3: Delaying breastfeeding risks her milk supply and is not NICE advice.

reteach.title: Count the flags, keep them together
reteach.question: Two habits answer most questions here: count the infection flags and factors, and ask whether the baby can stay with the mother. How do they work together?

blocks.body: Count: one red flag, or two other factors, means antibiotics within the hour without waiting for results. One factor means think and maybe watch for at least 12 hours. Place: if the baby is stable, transitional care lets the mother stay as the main carer while staff give IV antibiotics, tube feeds or phototherapy. The neonatal unit is for babies who are unstable or need intensive or high dependency care.

blocks.text: NG195 red flags are few: apnoea, seizures, CPR, ventilation, shock (in the baby) and infection in a co-twin (risk factor). Everything else is an 'other' factor that counts towards the two.

explain.body: Care additional to normal infant care, given in a postnatal setting by the resident mother with trained staff support. Typical candidates: 34+0-35+6 weeks, 1600-2000 g, stable babies on IV antibiotics, babies needing 3-hourly tube feeds, some phototherapy (BAPM 2017).

test.q: Who is the primary care provider for a baby in neonatal transitional care?
test.why: BAPM: NTC supports resident mothers as primary care providers, with trained healthcare professionals supporting them.

whyNot.0: Neonatal staff support, but the mother is the primary carer in transitional care.
whyNot.2: Doctors review the baby, but they are not the primary care provider.
whyNot.3: Health visitors work in the community after transfer from midwifery care.

explain.body: Box 1 risk factors (e.g. GBS, preterm labour, prolonged rupture of membranes, maternal sepsis, chorioamnionitis, co-twin infection) and box 2 indicators in the baby (red flags: apnoea, seizures, CPR, ventilation, shock).

test.q: Membranes ruptured 20 hours before the birth of a baby at 40 weeks. Under NG195, is this a risk factor for early-onset infection?
options: Yes, as it is over 18 hours
No, as term needs over 24 hours
No, as ROM is not a factor
test.why: NG195 box 1: confirmed rupture of membranes for more than 24 hours before a term birth (or more than 18 hours before a preterm birth).

whyNot.0: 18 hours applies to preterm births; at term the threshold is over 24 hours.
whyNot.1: Ruptured membranes count only beyond the time thresholds in box 1.
whyNot.3: Prolonged rupture of membranes is a listed risk factor once the threshold is met.

explain.body: Any red flag or 2+ other factors: investigate and give antibiotics within 1 hour of the decision, without waiting for results. Benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin. One factor: clinical judgement; monitor at least 12 hours if needed. Stop at 36 hours if cultures are negative, suspicion was not strong, the baby is well and CRP is reassuring (1.21.3).

test.q: A decision is made to start antibiotics for a baby with suspected early-onset infection. Within what time should they be given?
test.why: NG195 1.15.2: give antibiotics as soon as possible and always within 1 hour of the decision to treat.

whyNot.2: 6 hours is far too long for suspected neonatal sepsis.
whyNot.3: 12 hours is the minimum monitoring period for one risk factor, not an antibiotic deadline.

explain.body: At-risk babies: first glucose before the second feed (2-4 h), feeds no more than 3 hours apart, stay at least 24 hours. Treat under 1.0, under 2.5 with signs, or more than two under 2.0; gel for 1.0-1.9. NEWTT2: 1 repeat in 1 h; 2-3 review in 1 h; 4-5 within 15 min; 6+ immediate; concern can trigger review at any score.

head: Glucose (mmol/L)
Trigger
rows: More than two values, no signs

test.q: A midwife is worried about a baby whose NEWTT2 score is 0. What does the framework allow?
options: No review until the score rises
Wait for the next routine check
Ask the parents to watch overnight
test.why: NEWTT2: professional concern can trigger a review at any score.

whyNot.1: The framework lets concern trigger review whatever the score.
whyNot.2: Concern should be acted on now, not deferred.
whyNot.3: Parents should be involved, but the midwife's concern needs escalation.
